opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, less than people might expect. I think there's a narrative out there that if you believe AI is moving fast, you should be dramatically reorganizing your life: quitting things, stockpiling, assuming the world ends in five years. I don't really live that way.

What it has changed is my sense of urgency about the work itself. When you're close to the technology, you see how much value is still sitting on the table. The models are capable, but most of the world hasn't actually adopted them in a meaningful way yet. So for me the faster pace is less "the singularity is coming" and more "there's an enormous amount of practical work to do to get this into the hands of businesses, governments, and people, and to do it responsibly." That keeps me pretty focused.

On the personal side, I think about my kids' future differently. What skills matter, what education looks like when you have a tutor in your pocket that's better than anything we had growing up. I'm optimistic about that. I think the next generation will be extraordinarily empowered.

I try to stay grounded, too. I'm skeptical of the more extreme takes, whether doom or utopia. Progress is fast, but it's also bumpy and uneven, and the real world has a lot of friction. Deployment, trust, regulation, and integration all take time. So I hold both ideas at once: this is one of the most important technological shifts in history, and it's going to unfold through a lot of unglamorous, hard work rather than one dramatic moment.

r003.rationale: It rejects dramatic life changes in general, but does not specifically reject liquidating assets and vacationing permanently because of anticipated AI progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest shift for me has been a kind of compression of time horizons. When I was working on the transformer paper back at Google Brain, the future felt abstract. You'd think, "Maybe in a few decades we'll have systems that can really understand language." And now the timelines have collapsed so much that the thing you imagined as a lifetime project is something you're shipping to customers next quarter.

So on a personal level, I've become much more deliberate about what I spend my time on. I think a lot of people in this field have this feeling that the window to shape how this technology lands is relatively short. That's part of why I started Cohere, honestly. I didn't want to just sit back and watch a couple of labs decide how enterprises and governments get access to this stuff. I wanted to build something where businesses could actually own their deployment, keep their data, and not be beholden to a single provider.

But I'll also say I try not to get swept up in the apocalyptic or the utopian framing. I think both of those narratives tend to absolve people of responsibility. If it's inevitable doom, nothing matters. If it's inevitable utopia, nothing matters either. The reality is much more boring and much more important: it's a series of engineering decisions, product decisions, policy decisions, and every one of them is a place where humans get to choose.

So how has it changed how I think about the future? I guess I feel more urgency and more agency at the same time. I'm less interested in predicting what the world looks like in 2040 and more interested in getting the next two years right. And day to day, I'm trying to be a bit more present with people. I do think a lot of knowledge work is going to change, and that creates real anxiety for folks. I don't want to be someone who builds the thing and is dismissive of what it means for everyone else.

r002.rationale: The response rejects “inevitable utopia” as a framing and says it does not absolve people of responsibility.

astra-6.text:
It’s made the future feel a lot less fixed. I’m more cautious about assuming that the way something works today is how it’ll work in five or ten years. That’s exciting, but it also makes long-term planning harder.

I don’t think the right response is to put your life on hold while you wait for some enormous change. You still have to build relationships and do work you care about. For me, it’s more about staying adaptable—and, in the work itself, thinking carefully about what we’re building and whether it’s actually helping people.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s made the future feel a lot less predictable. I’m hesitant to make confident claims about what life will look like ten or twenty years from now, because so much depends on what we build and how people choose to use it.

But I don’t think the response should be to put your life on hold. You still have relationships, things you care about, things you want to do. For me, it creates a sense of urgency around the work: there’s an opportunity to build something useful, and a responsibility to get it right. You have to balance that urgency with staying grounded in the life you’re actually living.
